<reason>Side A won decisively through superior responsiveness, sharper comparative weighing, and concrete institutional grounding. While Side B relied heavily on repeating the anatomical distinction between cortical computation and embodied pain, Side A systematically neutralized each of B's core objections: explaining how microelectrode arrays bypass peripheral nociceptors to deliver aversive stimulation directly to central tissue, showing that passive Alzheimer's and ALS organoids would never trigger the learning threshold (a point Side B quietly dropped), and demonstrating how the Three Rs practically govern closed-loop protocols. Side B grew repetitive in the second half and leaned on an unpersuasive slippery-slope claim about computer algorithms, which Side A neatly turned against B in the closing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [A5.3], Side A dismantled Side B's warning in [B4.4] that triggering review for learning would force committees to regulate computer algorithms—pointing out that the trigger applies strictly to biological tissue and that swapping living neural cultures for computer algorithms is literally "Replacement," the first pillar of the Three Rs.</best_rebuttal>
